Understanding Private Health Insurance
What does private health insurance cover?
There are two types of private health insurance:
Hospital insurance, which covers all or some of the costs of hospital treatment as a private patient including doctor’s charges and hospital accommodation.
Extras insurance (also called ancillary), which covers treatments generally not available under Medicare like dental, optical, physiotherapy, chiropractic and acupuncture.
You can purchase hospital-only insurance, extras-only insurance, or combined hospital plus extras cover.
As a general rule, the more expensive the health cover you choose, the more hospital procedures and extras treatments will be included and the more money you’ll get back when you claim.
Why should I buy private health insurance?
Private health insurance offers you increased choice, convenience and flexibility.
With private hospital cover, you can be treated in a private or public hospital as a private patient. That means that you may be able to choose the doctor that treats you, the hospital you are treated in, and a time for treatment that suits you.
Private insurance also provides “extras” cover for services generally not included under Medicare like dental, optical, physiotherapy,
chiropractic, remedial massage and acupuncture. Many people use their private health cover to get access to services they may otherwise not be able to afford.
And last, but certainly not least, depending on your income, buying private hospital cover may help you to minimise your tax by avoiding having to pay the Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS). Single parents and couples (including de facto couples) are subject to family income thresholds.
See Surcharges, loadings and rebates to find out more
What should I look for when choosing health insurance?
When it comes to private health insurance, you’ll find that cheapest does not always equal best value. In fact, paying just a little extra each month can actually save you money, because you may be covered for more services that you’ll actually use.
When shopping for health insurance, some of the things you should look at include:
What services are included and excluded?
What restrictions apply to your cover?
How much can you get back for the services you’re most likely to use?
What waiting periods apply before you can claim?
How easy is it to make a claim?
Can you still see your favourite doctors and specialists?
Do you still get the same amount back if your doctor/specialist isn’t part of the fund’s preferred “network” of providers?
What private hospitals can you go to?
Is a “gap cover” scheme available?
What excess is payable for hospital visits and how many times each year does an excess apply?
Am I covered as soon as I take out private health insurance?
When you first buy private health insurance, or when you upgrade to a higher level of cover, you may have to wait some time before you are able to claim. These waiting periods apply to both hospital and extras.
Most private health funds recognise the waiting periods you’ve served with your previous insurer. That means that when you transfer to a level of insurance with the same (or lower) level of cover, as long as you transfer within 30 days of leaving your previous fund, you won’t need to re-serve waiting periods that you’ve already completed.
Is it easy to transfer between health insurance funds?
Yes, it is easy to transfer between health insurance funds. You can change insurance policies at any time: from one fund to another or even changing to a higher or lower level of cover within the same health fund.
You'll receive continuous cover if you transfer to Australian Unity within 30 days of leaving your previous fund. And if you switch to an equal (or lower) level of cover, you won't have to re-serve any waiting periods you've already completed.
The old fund will provide your new fund with a transfer certificate, which provides details about your level of cover, waiting periods already served, a history of recent claims, and any Lifetime Health Cover Loading that applies.
This information may also be used to adjust the annual and lifetime claim limits on your new policy. For example, if you've made $900 worth of orthodontics claims on your old cover, and your new policy has a $2400 lifetime claim limit, that $900 will be deducted from your new policy ($2400 - $900 = $1500) to reflect your true available limit.
Find out more about switching to Australian Unity.
Where can I find out more?
Head on over to our Health Insurance FAQs page to find more information on private health insurance, joining a health fund, surcharges, loadings and rebates. If you've got a specific question that we haven't answered here, call us on 1800 760 719. We're available Monday to Friday from 8:30am until 6:00pm AET excluding public holidays.
Here at Australian Unity, we offer a range of hospital and extras covers that you can mix-and-match to find the combination that best suits your changing needs.

Common Questions about Singles Health Insurance
What’s included in Singles health insurance cover?
Singles health insurance covers only one person of any age, and can include hospital cover, extras cover, or both—depending on the products you choose. Hospital cover helps with the cost of treatment as a private patient in hospital, while extras cover can help with services like dental, optical, and physio. Coverage levels vary by tier—Basic, Bronze, Silver, and Gold for hospital, and low, medium, or top for extras.
How much does Singles health insurance cover cost?
Singles health insurance policies are generally cheaper than couples or family health cover, as they only insure one person. The cost for hospital covers varies based on the level of cover—Basic, Bronze, Silver or Gold—and the excess you choose. Adding extras or selecting a combination cover will increase the price, depending on the services included. To find a health cover insurance that suits your needs, click ‘Get a Quote’.
How long am I eligible to be on my parents’ health insurance?
You can be covered as a dependant on your parents’ policy until you turn 23, whether you’re working or studying. From 23 to 30 (inclusive), you can stay on the family policy as a student dependant at no extra cost while enrolled in an approved full-time course.
If you’re not studying full-time, you may still be eligible to stay on the policy as a non-student dependant, though additional costs may apply.
Should couples get joint health insurance or separate Single policies?
It depends on your individual needs. Some couples find a joint policy more convenient, while others prefer separate Singles policies—especially when their health or lifestyle needs differ. The best option is the one that suits both your health and budget preferences.
Can Singles health insurance help me avoid the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
Yes, it can. For singles, holding at least a basic hospital policy with an excess of $750 or less can help you avoid the Medicare Levy Surcharge. For more information visit here.
How do I choose the right Singles health insurance cover?
We know everyone’s needs are different. That’s why we have a range of covers to suit your needs. To compare our range of health insurance options click here or call us on 1800 760 719 to speak with one of our private health insurance specialists. We’ll take care of everything, even cancelling your current policy.
I have a pre-existing health condition. Am I eligible for Singles health cover?
Yes, you are. Australian Unity’s hospital covers include a 12-month waiting period for hospital treatment related to pre-existing conditions. This applies to new members previously uninsured, as well as those who join us with a gap of 31 or more days from their previous insurer, or those upgrading to a higher level of cover. Go to pre-existing condition for further information.
Our extras covers do not have waiting periods for pre-existing conditions, only the standard waiting periods as listed on the product’s fact sheet.
Is it worth getting extras cover if I’m single?
Extras cover is a great option if you want help managing the cost of treatments generally not covered by Medicare, such as dental, optical, physiotherapy, chiropractic and acupuncture. Whether it’s right for you depends on how often you use these services. To explore extras options and find a cover that suits you, click ‘Get a Quote’.

Common Questions about Couples Health Insurance
How is the cost of a Couples’ policy calculated?
Couples’ policies are generally priced at twice the premium of a Singles policy, as they provide cover for two adults. The exact amount may vary depending on the level of cover and other policy features.
How is LHC loading calculated for Couples’ policies?
If you and your partner have been without cover for different lengths of time, your Lifetime Health Cover loading will be calculated by averaging out the two. For example, if you’re paying a 4% loading, and your partner has a 10% loading, that will be averaged out to 7% on a couple or family policy. For more information visit here.
What’s the Australian Government Rebate for couples?
To be able to claim the Government Rebate, both adults on the policy must be eligible for Medicare benefits. For Couples / Families policies we will apply the rebate percentage based on the oldest person on the membership.
Can dependents be added to a Couples’ policy?
Adding dependents will require changing your policy to a Family (including Single Parent Family) policy. This change will result in a higher premium, as the cover is expanded to include more people. In some cases, you may also need to switch to a different product, as some policies are not designed to cover more than two adults. To review your options and find a cover that suits your family, click ‘Get a Quote’.
Can my partner be added to my existing policy?
Yes, generally you can add your partner to your policy. This may result in a higher premium, as the cover is expanded to include another person if you are on a Single or Single Parent membership. To explore your options and find a suitable policy, click ‘Get a Quote’.
Is it possible to share health insurance after divorce?
It’s possible to remain on the same membership following a separation or divorce. Please keep in mind that any claim payments will be paid into the account listed under the membership, regardless of who paid for the treatment. If any disputes arise we will keep the agreement with the person who holds authority over the membership. Unless advised otherwise, the spouse named on the membership will have automatic delegated authority.
Do I have to be married to get couples health cover policy?
You can add your partner regardless of your marital status. Policy Holder’s Partner means a legally married spouse of, or a person in a De Facto Relationship with, the Policy Holder;
How do I switch to Australian Unity?
Switching private health insurance from another fund is simple — just get a quote and join online, or call us on 1800 760 719 to speak with one of our experts. We’ll take care of the rest, including cancelling your existing policy.

Common Questions about Family Health Insurance
How can private health insurance support my family's healthcare needs?
Private health insurance can help your family access a wider range of healthcare services, reduce wait times for hospital treatment, and cover everyday health needs like dental, optical, and physio. Read more to learn how it can support your family.
Who can be on a Family health insurance policy?
Family cover includes two adults—the policyholder and their spouse or partner—plus their dependants, who can stay on the policy up to 30 years of age (subject to eligibility).
How expensive is Family health insurance?
Family health insurance is generally the most expensive membership scale, as it’s designed to insure two adults and their children under one policy. Costs of hospital covers vary depending on the level of cover—Basic, Bronze, Silver or Gold—and the excess you choose.
Adding extras or selecting a combination cover can increase the price, depending on the services included. To find a cover that suits your family’s needs, click ‘Get a Quote’.
What discounts and rewards are on offer?
We offer a variety of incentives to our members such as the Wellplan Rewards program, providing discounts to a large range of services and entertainment. We also provide a 4% discount to any members that pay their premiums via direct debit. Check out here for more details.
Can I update my cover if my family situation changes?
Yes, you can. We understand that life changes and your private health insurance cover should be able to change with it. That’s why we make it easy for you to switch between covers that better suit your lifestyle. Simply give us a call on 1800 760 719, and we’ll take care of the rest. It is important to contact us as soon as possible as we may not be able to process your request for an earlier date.
At what point do children need their own health insurance policy?
Children can stay on a Family policy as dependants until they turn 23, whether they’re working or studying. From 23 to 30 (inclusive), they may remain on the policy as student dependants at no extra cost if they’re enrolled in an approved full-time course. If they’re not studying full-time, they may still be eligible to stay on as non-student dependants, though additional costs may apply.
Is pregnancy covered under Family health insurance?
Not necessarily. “Family” refers to who’s covered under the policy—not what’s included. To be covered for pregnancy and birth-related services, you’ll need to choose a hospital policy that includes those specific benefits. Go here to find the right level of cover for your needs.
How do I choose the right level of Family health cover?
We know everyone’s needs are different. That’s why we have a range of covers to suit you and your loved ones’ needs. To compare our range of health insurance options click here or call us on 1800 760 719 to speak with one of our private health insurance specialists. We’ll take care of everything, even cancelling your current policy.
Can Family health insurance help me avoid the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
Yes, it can. Holding at least a basic hospital policy with an excess of $750 or less can help you avoid the Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS). To find a cover that suits your needs, click Get a Quote.
Can I get pregnancy cover without a waiting period?
No, pregnancy and birth-related services are subject to a 12-month waiting period on hospital covers that include these benefits. This means you will need to have an eligible private health insurance policy for at least 12 months before you can claim for these services.

Common Questions about Single Parents Health Insurance
Who can be included on Single Parent cover?
Whether it’s big kids or little kids, we offer a range of affordable options to help look after your family’s health. Single parent family cover includes one adult and their dependent children. Dependant children up to 23 are covered under our Single parent health cover at no extra cost. Once they turn 23, we can continue to cover them until they turn 31 if they are not married or living in a de facto relationship.
They can be covered as a student dependant while studying full-time, or, if they are not studying full-time, we can still cover them as a non-student dependant with an increase in premium. To find a cover that suits your family’s needs, click ‘Get a Quote’.
Who is considered a Dependant?
A Dependant is a:
natural child (including newborns);
legally adopted child
stepchild;
foster child;
of the Policy Holder and/or Policy Holder’s Partner who is covered under the membership.
What should I look for in Single parent health insurance cover?
It’s worth checking whether the policy includes additional benefits for your children—such as no excess or co-payments for hospital admissions for your dependants and school accident top-up benefits. Some extras have family annual limits, meaning the annual limit for some services is shared by everyone on the policy. Also, if your children are aged 23–30, whether they are studying full-time can affect your premium.
What’s the difference between Single parent and Family health insurance?
Single parent cover is for one adult and their dependants, with children covered up to 30 years of age. Family health insurance cover includes two adults—the policyholder and their spouse/partner—plus dependants up to 30 years of age.
Can Single parent health insurance help avoid the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
Yes, it can. Any adult, including those on Single parent family cover, who holds at least a basic hospital policy (including our cheapest hospital cover) with an excess of $750 or less may be exempt from the surcharge. For more information, visit here.
I have a pre-existing health condition. Am I eligible for Single parent health cover?
Yes, you are. Australian Unity’s hospital covers include a 12-month waiting period for hospital treatment related to pre-existing conditions. This applies to new members previously uninsured, as well as those who join us with a gap of 31 or more days from their previous insurer, or those upgrading to a higher level of cover.
Go to pre-existing condition for further information. Our extras covers do not have waiting periods for pre-existing conditions, only the standard waiting periods as listed on the product’s Fact Sheet.
Can a married couple have different health insurance policies?
Yes, they can. Couples may choose to hold separate Single or Single parent policies instead of a joint Couple or Family policy—it all depends on what suits their individual needs best. To find a cover that suits your family’s needs, click ‘Get a Quote’.
I want to join Australian Unity – how do I switch from my current fund?
Switching to Australian Unity is simple and secure. All you need to do is call us on 1300 899 304 or sign up online and let us know you’re switching. We’ll handle the rest—with your permission, we’ll contact your previous fund to arrange cancellation and transfer your membership details so you don’t need to re-serve waiting periods or lose any Lifetime Health Cover status.
You’ll enjoy continuous cover, and if you change your mind within 30 days and haven’t made any claims, you can cancel and get your money back.
Can I update my cover if my family situation changes?
We understand that life changes and your cover should be able to change with it. That’s why we make it easy for you to switch between covers that better suit your lifestyle. Simply give us a call on 1800 760 719, and we’ll take care of the rest. It is important to contact us as soon as possible as we may not be able to process your request for an earlier date.
What steps should I take with my health insurance if I separate from my partner?
If you are on a Family Policy, you can remove them from your membership. Simply give us a call on 1800 760 719 to make this change. It’s important to contact us as we may not be able to process your request for an earlier date. It’s possible to remain on the same membership following a separation or divorce.
Please keep in mind that any claim payments will be paid into the account listed under the membership, regardless of who paid for the treatment. If any disputes arise we will keep the agreement with the person who holds authority over the membership. Unless advised otherwise, the spouse named on the membership will have automatic delegated authority.
Can Single Parents receive a government subsidy for health insurance?
Health insurance for Single parents is priced with affordability in mind. These policies are designed to provide quality cover for you and your children—often at a lower cost than standard family health insurance policies.
With all our policies, including Single Parents, you may be eligible for the Australian Government Private Health Insurance Rebate, where depending on your circumstances, the government will subsidise a portion of your health insurance premiums.

Understanding your Hospital Cover
Waiting periods
A waiting period is the amount of time you have to wait after joining or upgrading until you can make a claim for a service or treatment.
Hospital excess
Excess is the additional amount you agree to pay towards accommodation costs if you need hospital treatment. Please refer to your product Fact Sheet for details about the maximum excess payable in a calendar year and any excess waivers that may apply.
Pre-existing conditions
A pre-existing condition is an ailment, illness or condition that in the opinion of a medical practitioner appointed by Australian Unity (not your own doctor), the signs or symptoms of that ailment, illness or condition existed at any time in the period of six months ending on the day on which you joined Australian Unity or upgraded your cover, irrespective of whether you were aware of it. If you make a hospital claim in the first 12 months of your joining or upgrading your cover, we will ask you to get your consulting doctors or other practitioner (e.g. your dentist, GP or specialist) to complete a medical report. You should ask us to carry out this assessment before going into hospital.
Accidents
Accident means an unplanned and unforeseen event, occurring by chance, and leading to bodily injuries caused solely and directly by an external force or object requiring treatment from a Medical Practitioner (defined here as a medical doctor who is not the member or a relative of the Member) within 7 days of the event, but excludes injuries arising out of: surgical procedures; unforeseen illness; pregnancy; drug use; and aggravation of an underlying condition or injury.
Restricted
Restricted services are hospital claims which are limited to a minimum (default) benefit. This is the minimum dollar amount set by the Australian Government for accommodation as a private patient in a shared room of a public hospital. A Restricted service does not pay any money towards the cost of intensive or coronary care, labour ward or theatre fees in a private hospital or private day centre. Therefore you may incur a large out-of-pocket expense. Contact us for more information.
Exclusions
If you select a hospital cover that has treatments listed as ‘Excluded’ or 'Not Covered', this means that we will not pay any benefits for the treatment you have received and this can result in you incurring large out-of-pocket costs. Always refer to your product Fact Sheet for more details about your hospital cover entitlements.
Out-of-pocket costs
If you are admitted to hospital (including for Covered treatments) you may have out-of-pocket costs, e.g. an excess, a ‘gap’ in your doctors’ medical bills, emergency department fees, or the additional cost of a private room in a public or non-agreement hospital. If you want more specific information about what you can expect these costs to be, we recommend you obtain a quote from your doctors/hospital before undergoing treatment. Then contact us for details of benefits before proceeding with your treatment. Additionally, benefits are not payable for claims where you have the right to claim compensation, damages or benefits from another source (e.g. TAC or WorkCover), now or at a later date.
Understanding your Extras Cover
Waiting periods
Preventative Health Services
Preventative Health Services can offer practical support to help bring about positive change in members’ lives to help you get and stay healthy. They include things like losing weight, getting fit, quitting smoking, and working with a health coach to improve your general health and wellbeing. You’ll receive personalised and practical support plus information designed to bring about positive change giving you the tools needed to enjoy a longer, healthier and happier life.
To check your eligibility, which providers and programs you are able to use and any waiting periods that may apply, please contact us on 13 29 39. More information can be found here.
Where an Extras cover is taken with Hospital cover, benefits are payable under the Hospital cover only.
Out-of-pocket costs
Extras cover can help you get money back on common health treatments that aren’t generally covered by Medicare. You’ll get either a percentage of the cost back, or a set dollar amount, on included Extras every time you claim, until you reach your yearly limit. Therefore, you only pay the difference between what you get back from Australian Unity and the cost set by your provider.
Please call us or refer to your Member Guide and Terms & Conditions for further information on how this cover works. If you want more specific information about what you can expect your out-of-pocket costs to be, we recommend you obtain a quote from your provider before undergoing treatment, along with a list of item numbers. You can then contact us or log in to Online Member Services for details of benefits before proceeding with your treatment.
Recognised providers
We only pay benefits when you see a recognised provider in a private practice. Please contact us to check if your provider is recognised by us. Providers recognition conditions apply.

For example: surgery to remove wisdom teeth, and dental implant surgery.
Digestive system

For example: torn tendons, rotator cuff tears and damaged ligaments.

Bone fractures are listed separately under bone, joint and muscle.
Procedures to the spinal column are listed separately under back, neck and spine.
Podiatric surgery performed by a registered podiatric surgeon is listed separately under podiatric surgery (provided by a registered podiatric surgeon).
Rehabilitation
Hospital treatment for physical rehabilitation for a patient related to surgery or illness.
For example: inpatient and admitted day patient rehabilitation, stroke recovery, cardiac rehabilitation.
Palliative care
Hospital treatment for care where the intent is primarily providing quality of life for a patient with a terminal illness, including treatment to alleviate and manage pain.
Hospital psychiatric services
Hospital treatment for the treatment and care of patients with psychiatric, mental, addiction or behavioural disorders.
For example: psychoses such as schizophrenia, mood disorders such as depression, eating disorders and addiction therapy.

Blood

For example: blood clotting disorders and bone marrow transplants.

Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of diseases, disorders and injuries of the musculoskeletal system.
For example: carpal tunnel, fractures, hand surgery, joint fusion, bone spurs, osteomyelitis and bone cancer.

Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of breast disorders and associated lymph nodes, and reconstruction and/or reduction following breast surgery or a preventative mastectomy.

Non-endoscopic procedures for the digestive system are listed separately under digestive system.
Gynaecology
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the female reproductive system.

Lung and chest
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the lungs, lung-related conditions, mediastinum and chest.

Male reproductive system
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the male reproductive system including the prostate.
For example: male sterilisation, circumcision and prostate cancer.
Miscarriage and termination of pregnancy
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of a miscarriage or for termination of pregnancy.

Hospital treatment for pain management that does not require the insertion or surgical management of a device.
For example: treatment of nerve pain and chest pain due to cancer by injection of a nerve block.

Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the back, neck and spinal column, including spinal fusion.

Hospital treatment for the implantation, replacement or other surgical management of a device required for the treatment of pain.

Hospital treatment which is medically necessary for the investigation and treatment of any physical deformity, whether acquired as a result of illness or Accident, or congenital.

Hospital treatment for investigation and treatment of conditions associated with pregnancy and child birth.

Hospital treatment for surgery that is designed to reduce a person's weight, remove excess skin due to weight loss and reversal of a bariatric procedure.
For example: gastric banding, gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy.

Play it smart this tax time with health insurance
Save up to 1.5% on income tax for FY27

Get hospital cover by age 31 to save on premiums later
You’ll need hospital cover by 1 July by your 31st birthday, to avoid paying higher premiums later, due to Lifetime Health Cover loading (LHC).
See how LHC works
Tax time FAQs
Do I need to have hospital cover for the full financial year to avoid paying MLS at tax time?
For many Australians, tax time and health cover are closely linked. To avoid paying the Medicare Levy Surcharge, an individual generally needs to hold eligible private hospital cover for the full financial year. The surcharge is applied based on the number of days without cover, which means that if a person takes out or cancels hospital cover part way through the year, they may still pay the surcharge for the days they were not covered.
Can private health insurance help reduce the tax I pay?
If an individual’s income is above the Medicare Levy Surcharge income threshold and they do not have eligible hospital cover, they may pay an additional tax of between 1 percent and 1.5 percent of their income. Taking out qualifying private hospital cover for the full financial year can help them avoid this surcharge. Depending on their situation, the cost of basic hospital cover can be similar to or less than the extra tax they would otherwise pay.
How do I include my health insurance details when lodging my tax return?
Each year, health funds provide policy holders with a tax statement that includes policy details, premiums and any Australian Government rebate received. These details are also lodged with the Australian Tax Office by health funds and are usually pre-filled in an online tax return when lodging through myTax or a registered tax agent. If they are not pre-filled, a member can enter the information from their statement manually. For specific tax or lodgment questions, please speak with the Australian Taxation Office or a registered tax agent.
I recently turned 31, do I need to consider taking out hospital cover?
Yes! The Lifetime Health Cover (LHC) loading is a charge applied to new policy holders that were not covered by an appropriate level of private hospital cover past the age of 31. It was introduced to encourage early adoption and maintenance of health insurance. All of Australian Unity’s hospital covers exempt members from paying the MLS.
Once you turn 31, you’ve got until the following 1 July to buy private hospital cover and avoid paying the LHC loading. For every year you delay, you may have to pay an additional 2% (up to a maximum of 70%) on top of the cost of your private hospital cover. The good news is that the loading doesn’t last a lifetime. Once you have held private hospital cover for 10 continuous years, the loading will be removed. For more information, visit Lifetime Health Cover Loading: What Is It? How Does It Work?
What income do I need to earn to pay the Medicare Levy Surcharge?
The Medicare Levy Surcharge generally applies if income for surcharge purposes is above certain thresholds and an individual does not have eligible private hospital cover. As a guide, from 1 July 2026, the surcharge may apply if a person is single and their annual income is above $105,000, or if they are part of a couple or family with a combined annual income above $210,000. The surcharge rate increases in tiers as income rises. For the latest thresholds and rates, it is important to check the Australian Taxation Office website or speak with a registered tax agent.
Can couples and families also save on tax with hospital cover?
Couples and families often ask how hospital cover fits into their broader wellbeing and financial plans. If a combined family income is above the Medicare Levy Surcharge threshold and there is no eligible private hospital cover for every family member, the household may pay the surcharge. Taking out an appropriate family or couples hospital policy and maintaining it for the full financial year for all members of the household can help avoid the surcharge. This can be especially important if there are dependent children, as the income thresholds may change based on the number of dependents. For more information please speak to a registered tax agent or visit the ATO website.
What is the private health insurance rebate?
The Australian Government private health insurance rebate is a government incentive to help Australians with the cost of private health insurance, and it is income tested, which means the level of rebate received may reduce or cease once income goes above certain thresholds. Different thresholds apply for singles and for couples or families. Rebate tiers are impacted both by income and age and are usually adjusted annually across the private health insurance sector for any payments made from 1 April. It is important to check the latest information on the Australian Taxation Office or PrivateHealth.gov.au websites. You can also speak with a registered tax agent for guidance.
How much tax can you save with private health insurance?
The potential tax saving from an eligible private hospital cover depends on taxable income and rebate tier. For some people, the cost of basic hospital cover can be similar to or less than the additional tax they might pay without cover. For advice tailored to a person’s circumstances, it is important to speak with a registered tax agent.
Is private health insurance only useful for tax purposes?
Private health insurance can have lots of tax implications depending on personal circumstances. Many people also value the real healthcare benefits it offers while navigating health events. These benefits can include reduced waiting times for elective surgery (private vs public system), more choice of doctor, healthcare provider and hospital, along with access to private hospital facilities. Over time, purchasing and maintaining hospital cover from age 31 can also help avoid charges like the Lifetime Health Cover loading.

Chemotherapy, radiotherapy and immunotherapy for cancer

Dental surgery
Hospital treatment for surgery to the teeth and gums.
For example: surgery to remove wisdom teeth, and dental implant surgery.
Digestive system
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the digestive system, including the oesophagus, stomach, gall bladder, pancreas, spleen, liver and bowel.
For example: oesophageal cancer, irritable bowel syndrome, gall stones and haemorrhoids.

For example: torn tendons, rotator cuff tears and damaged ligaments.

Bone fractures are listed separately under bone, joint and muscle.
Procedures to the spinal column are listed separately under back, neck and spine.
Podiatric surgery performed by a registered podiatric surgeon is listed separately under podiatric surgery (provided by a registered podiatric surgeon).
Rehabilitation
Hospital treatment for physical rehabilitation for a patient related to surgery or illness.
For example: inpatient and admitted day patient rehabilitation, stroke recovery, cardiac rehabilitation.
Palliative care
Hospital treatment for care where the intent is primarily providing quality of life for a patient with a terminal illness, including treatment to alleviate and manage pain.
Hospital psychiatric services
Hospital treatment for the treatment and care of patients with psychiatric, mental, addiction or behavioural disorders.
For example: psychoses such as schizophrenia, mood disorders such as depression, eating disorders and addiction therapy.

For example: blood clotting disorders and bone marrow transplants.

Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of diseases, disorders and injuries of the musculoskeletal system.
For example: carpal tunnel, fractures, hand surgery, joint fusion, bone spurs, osteomyelitis and bone cancer.

For example: stroke, brain or spinal cord tumours, head injuries, epilepsy and Parkinson's disease.

Breast surgery (medically necessary)
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of breast disorders and associated lymph nodes, and reconstruction and/or reduction following breast surgery or a preventative mastectomy.

Eyelid procedures are listed separately under plastic and reconstructive surgery.
Gastrointestinal endoscopy
Hospital treatment for the diagnosis, investigation and treatment of the internal parts of the gastrointestinal system using an endoscope.
For example: colonoscopy, gastroscopy, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
Non-endoscopic procedures for the digestive system are listed separately under digestive system.
Gynaecology
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the female reproductive system.
For example: endometriosis, polycystic ovaries, female sterilisation and cervical cancer.
Fertility treatments are listed separately under assisted reproductive services.
Pregnancy and birth-related conditions are listed separately under pregnancy and birth.
Miscarriage or termination of pregnancy is listed separately under miscarriage and termination of pregnancy.
Hernia and appendix
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of a hernia or appendicitis.
Digestive conditions are listed separately under digestive system.

Kidney and bladder
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the kidney, adrenal gland and bladder.
For example: kidney stones, adrenal gland tumour and incontinence.
Dialysis is listed separately under dialysis for chronic kidney failure.
Lung and chest
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the lungs, lung-related conditions, mediastinum and chest.
For example: lung cancer, respiratory disorders such as asthma, pneumonia, and treatment of trauma to the chest.
Male reproductive system
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the male reproductive system including the prostate.
For example: male sterilisation, circumcision and prostate cancer.
Miscarriage and termination of pregnancy
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of a miscarriage or for termination of pregnancy.
Pain management
Hospital treatment for pain management that does not require the insertion or surgical management of a device.
For example: treatment of nerve pain and chest pain due to cancer by injection of a nerve block.
Pain management using a device (for example an infusion pump or neurostimulator) is listed separately under pain management with device.
Skin
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of skin, skin-related conditions and nails. The removal of foreign bodies is also included. Plastic surgery that is medically necessary and relating to the treatment of a skin-related condition is also included.
For example: melanoma, minor wound repair and abscesses.
Removal of excess skin due to weight loss is listed separately under weight loss surgery.
Tonsils, adenoids and grommets
Hospital treatment of the tonsils, adenoids and insertion or removal of grommets.
Assisted reproductive services
Hospital treatment for fertility treatments or procedures.
For example: retrieval of eggs or sperm, In vitro Fertilisation (IVF), and Gamete Intra-fallopian Transfer (GIFT).
Treatment of the female reproductive system is listed separately under gynaecology.
Pregnancy and birth-related services are listed separately under pregnancy and birth.
Back, neck and spine
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the back, neck and spinal column, including spinal fusion.
For example: sciatica, prolapsed or herniated disc, spinal disc replacement and spine curvature disorders such as scoliosis, kyphosis and lordosis.
Joint fusions are listed separately under bone, joint and muscle.
Cataracts
Hospital treatment for surgery to remove a cataract and replace with an artificial lens.
Dialysis for chronic kidney failure
Hospital treatment for dialysis treatment for chronic kidney failure.
For example: peritoneal dialysis and haemodialysis.
Heart and vascular system
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of the heart, heart-related conditions and vascular system.
For example: heart failure and heart attack, monitoring of heart conditions, varicose veins and removal of plaque from arterial walls.
Implantation of hearing devices
Hospital treatment to correct hearing loss, including implantation of a prosthetic hearing device.
Stapedectomy is listed separately under ear, nose and throat.
Insulin pumps
Hospital treatment for the provision and replacement of insulin pumps for treatment of diabetes.
Joint replacements
Hospital treatment for surgery for joint replacements, including revisions, resurfacing, partial replacements and removal of prostheses.
For example: replacement of shoulder, wrist, finger, hip, knee, ankle, or toe joint.

Pain management with device
Hospital treatment for the implantation, replacement or other surgical management of a device required for the treatment of pain.

Plastic and reconstructive surgery (medically necessary)
Hospital treatment which is medically necessary for the investigation and treatment of any physical deformity, whether acquired as a result of illness or Accident, or congenital.
For example: burns requiring a graft, cleft palate, club foot and angioma.
Plastic surgery that is medically necessary relating to the treatment of a skin-related condition is listed separately under skin.
Podiatric surgery (provided by a registered surgical podiatrist)
Hospital treatment for the investigation and treatment of conditions affecting the foot and/or ankle, provided by a registered surgical podiatrist, but limited to cover for:
accommodation; and
the cost of a prosthesis as listed in the prostheses list set out in the Private Health Insurance (Prostheses) Rules, as in force from time to time.

Pregnancy and birth
Hospital treatment for investigation and treatment of conditions associated with pregnancy and child birth.
Treatment for the baby is covered under the clinical category relevant to their condition (provided your baby is included under your cover). For example, respiratory conditions are covered under lung and chest.
Female reproductive conditions are listed separately under gynaecology.
Miscarriage and termination of pregnancy is listed separately under miscarriage and termination of pregnancy.
Sleep studies
Hospital treatment for the investigation of sleep patterns and anomalies.
For example: sleep apnoea and snoring.
Weight loss surgery
Hospital treatment for surgery that is designed to reduce a person's weight, remove excess skin due to weight loss and reversal of a bariatric procedure.
For example: gastric banding, gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy.

Frequently asked questions
What is the best health insurance for people over 50?
The best health insurance for people over 50 isn't necessarily the most expensive. It's the cover that best reflects your health needs, lifestyle and stage of life.
Many Australians review their health insurance after 50 as their priorities evolve. Things like heart health, joint replacements, cataracts, prevention and recovery often become more important, while other benefits may become less relevant.
That's why we developed a range of products specifically for different stages of life after 50. Using member insights, research and claims data, we've focused on providing age-relevant value, helping people pay for more of what they may use and less of what they may not.
What health insurance benefits become more important after 50?
Everyone's needs are different, but many people find their health priorities start to change after 50. Things like heart health, mobility, vision, prevention and recovery often become more important, while other benefits may become less relevant.
Common areas people look for in health cover after 50 include:
Heart and cardiovascular treatment
Joint replacements and mobility support, including hip and knee-related treatments
Cataract surgery and eye health
Back and spine treatment
Dental care, including fillings, crowns and root canal treatment
Prevention and early detection support, such as skin cancer checks, gym memberships and bone density scans
Rehabilitation and recovery programs, including initiatives that may help improve strength, mobility and recovery after illness, injury or surgery
Many people look for health insurance that helps them stay active and independent for longer, which may include programs such as the Kieser Hip & Knee Osteoarthritis Program and services like Hospital at Home, allowing eligible members to receive approved treatments, such as chemotherapy or rehabilitation, in the comfort of their own home.
The right cover isn't necessarily the most expensive. It's the cover that reflects your health needs today, while providing confidence for what you may need in the future.
What health cover should I consider before retirement?
As retirement approaches, many Australians review their health insurance to make sure it still reflects their health needs, lifestyle and budget. While getting value from your cover becomes more important as you move towards a fixed income, it's also important to have confidence you're covered for the treatments you're most likely to need.
Many people look for cover that includes things like heart health, joint replacements, cataract surgery, prevention and recovery support, without paying for benefits that may be less relevant at this stage of life.
The goal isn't necessarily to spend less or have more cover. It's to find the right balance between value and protection, so you can continue to access the treatment you want, when you need it, without unexpected costs or gaps in cover.
Is Gold health insurance worth it?
Gold health insurance can be worthwhile for some people, particularly if they want cover for every hospital treatment recognised by the private health insurance system. However, others may find better value in products that focus on the treatments and services most relevant to their needs.
It's also important to understand that Gold cover doesn't provide a higher standard of treatment. If a treatment is covered by your policy, you'll generally receive the same care whether you have Gold, Silver Plus or Bronze cover. The difference is which treatments are included, not the quality of treatment you receive.
Many of our products are Silver Plus, which means they include all Silver hospital benefits plus selected higher-level treatments that are often important to people over 50, such as joint replacements and cataract surgery. This allows us to focus on the treatments our member insights, research and claims data suggest are most relevant to this stage of life, helping deliver Gold-level peace of mind where it matters most, without the cost of paying for every possible treatment category.
For many people, the question isn't whether a policy is Gold or Silver Plus. It's whether it covers the treatments they're most likely to need and provides good value for money.
What makes a health insurance product tailored to people over 50?
Silver Plus products include all Silver hospital benefits plus additional treatments selected by the health fund. Importantly, not all Silver Plus products are the same. Different funds include different higher-level treatments, so it's important to look at what's actually covered rather than just the product tier.
For example, one Silver Plus product may include treatments that are more relevant to younger families, while another may focus on treatments that become more common later in life.
We designed our Silver Plus products using member insights, research and claims data to better reflect the needs of people over 50. That's why our range includes higher-level treatments such as joint replacements, cataract surgery, heart and cardiovascular care, and dialysis for chronic kidney failure, while excluding some treatments that are less relevant to many people at this stage of life.
For many people, it's a smarter way to access broad hospital cover. Rather than paying for every possible treatment, our approach focuses on providing strong cover for the treatments people over 50 are most likely to need and balancing the cost.
I'm 60 and don't need pregnancy cover. What health insurance should I look for?
Many people in their 60s look for cover that focuses on the treatments and services they are more likely to use, rather than paying for benefits that may no longer feel relevant, such as pregnancy and birth-related services, which are typically included in Gold tier hospital cover.
Our new Silver Plus range is designed to include a range of higher-tier services that may be more relevant at this life stage, such as cataracts, joint replacements and dialysis.
What is the best value health insurance for over 50s?
The best value health insurance for people over 50 isn't necessarily the cheapest or the most expensive. For many Australians, value means having cover for the treatments, services and benefits they're most likely to use, without paying for things that may be less relevant to this stage of life.
As health needs change, many people start looking for cover that includes things like heart and cardiovascular treatment, joint replacements, cataract surgery and support for managing chronic health conditions. Extras benefits may also become more important, particularly for major dental work such as crowns, root canals and implants, hearing aids, optical services and skin cancer checks.
Many people also look for ways to help manage out-of-pocket costs through lower excesses, gap cover arrangements and strong extras benefits.
That's why we developed our range of cover for life after 50. Using member insights, research and claims data, we've designed products around the health needs and priorities that often become more relevant after 50, rather than trying to create one product designed to suit everyone.
For many people, value comes from paying for more of what they're likely to use and less of what they're not.
Is seniors health insurance different from health insurance for over 50s?
"Seniors health insurance" is often used as a broad term for health cover aimed at older Australians, particularly those approaching or are in retirement. However, there isn't a single age at which someone becomes a "senior", and different organisations use different age thresholds.
What's more important than the label is whether your cover reflects your current stage of life. Many people start reviewing their health insurance in their 50s as their health needs, priorities and financial goals begin to change.
That's why our range has been designed around life after 50, recognising that what matters at 50 may not be the same as what matters at 60 or 70. The focus is on providing relevant cover, value and confidence through each stage, as your needs evolve and not a one sizes fits all.

title: Reciprocal Health Care Agreements (RHCA)
text:
Health Insurance
Overseas Visitors Cover
About Overseas Visitors Cover
Reciprocal Health Care Agreements (RHCAs)
Reciprocal Health Care Agreements (RHCA)
Traveling abroad can be a thrilling experience, but unexpected illness or injury can quickly dampen the excitement.
Fortunately, if you are visiting our beautiful country from one of the countries Australia has a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement with you may be eligible to receive some essential medical treatments through our public healthcare system and reduce out-of-pocket expenses for necessary healthcare while overseas.
Medicare and Reciprocal Health Care Agreements
Medicare is the publicly funded universal health care insurance scheme in Australia. The scheme either partially or fully covers the cost of most health care, with services being delivered by state and territory governments or private enterprises.
Enrolment in Medicare is not just for Australian citizens and permanent residents. International visitors from 11 countries that have Reciprocal Health Care Agreements are partially or fully covered under Medicare for medically necessary treatment.
The Reciprocal Health Care Agreements allow eligible visitors to access essential medical care while in Australia—and at the same time enable Australians to receive similar care when visiting these countries.
Which countries have a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement with Australia, and what healthcare services can visitors from these countries access?
If you're visiting from one of the Reciprocal Health Care Agreement countries, you may be entitled to:
Medically necessary treatment
Including:
As a public patient in a public hospital for urgent care for illnesses or injuries that cannot wait until you return home.
Out of hospital services covered by Medicare.
Subsidised prescription medicines
Under the:
Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS)
To access these benefits, you’ll need to enrol in Medicare and receive your Medicare card.
To see exactly what you're entitled to, and what are the requirements to apply for your Medicare card please select the country you're visiting from using the links below:
Belgium
Finland
Italy
Malta
Nether
lands
New Zealand
Norway
Ireland
Slovenia
Sweden
United Kingdom
Want extra peace of mind beyond what Medicare covers?
Medicare offers limited coverage under the Reciprocal Health Care Agreements, but you don't have to stop there.
With Australian Unity, you can enhance your protection with additional cover options:
Overseas Visitors Hospital Cover (OVHC)
Ideal if you want broader medical protection, including access to private hospital care, ambulance cover and more. We have a range of hospital covers for those who are working or those who are just vising for holidays.
Looking to buy Overseas Visitor Cover?
Get a quote
Extras Cover
Get support for everyday health needs outside the hospital or GP’s clinics, not covered by Medicare, such as dental, physiotherapy, optical, and more.
The good news? If you hold a Medicare card, you may be eligible to reduce the premiums on your Extras Cover by applying for the Australian Government Rebate on private health insurance. This rebate is income-tested and can help make your cover more affordable.
Looking to buy an Extras Cover?
Get a quote
Do you earn income in Australia?
If you're an overseas visitor covered under a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement and earning income in Australia, you may be subject to the Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS)—just like Australian residents. The MLS is an additional tax applied to higher-income earners who do not hold eligible private hospital cover.
Important
Having an Overseas Visitors Health Cover (OVHC) does not exempt you from the MLS
If your tax advisor or another professional has informed you that you're liable for the surcharge, you may be able to avoid it by purchasing a Complying Health Insurance Policy (CHIP) with Australian Unity.
Do I need both an OVHC and CHIP product?
What’s best for you really depends on your personal circumstances and what level of cover you’re looking for:
CHIP: This type of cover is designed to meet the tax requirements for MLS exemption. It does not provide access to medical or hospital services to overseas visitors, as it’s intended for Australian residents only. Looking to avoid MLS? Get a quote
OVHC: If you need actual medical or hospital cover beyond what a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement provides, you’ll need to purchase OVHC separately.
The good news?
You can choose the lowest-cost CHIP hospital cover from Australian Unity to meet the MLS exemption requirement. Plus, depending on your income, you may be eligible for the Australian Government Rebate on private health insurance, which can help reduce your premiums. Be sure to have your Medicare card handy when applying for the rebate - it's required as part of the process.

title: Waiting periods
text:
Health Insurance
Overseas Visitors Cover
About Overseas Visitors Cover
What is a waiting period?
Waiting periods
A waiting period is the amount of time you have to wait before you can start to claim on your health insurance. Waiting periods apply to both hospital and extras covers and you cannot claim for procedures/services that you receive during a waiting period.
Waiting periods apply when you join, upgrade your cover, reduce your excess or re-join after a break in cover. The period you may need to wait varies depending on the level of cover you’ve chosen, and in the case of Working Visa Covers, whether you were insured previously. Check your product fact sheet for full details about your selected cover.
If you have Private Health Insurance (for Australian citizens and permanent residents), you can find out about waiting periods here.
Waiting periods
The following waiting periods apply to Australian Unity hospital covers. It is important to note that the benefits payable for these procedures can vary depending on your level of cover, and some procedures may be excluded or restricted. Check your product fact sheet for full details about your selected cover.
Working visa cover waiting periods
Level of cover | Waiting periods
Budget Workers cover | 2 months for psychiatric, rehabilitation and palliative care 12 months for preganancy and related services 12 months for all pre-existing conditions except psychiatric, rehabilitation and palliative care
Mid Workers Cover & Workers Cover Plus | 2 months for psychiatric, rehabilitation and palliative care 2 months for out-of-hospital pharmacy 12 months for pregnancy and related services 12 months for all pre-existing conditions except psychiatric, rehabilitation and palliative care
Non-working and working holiday visa cover waiting periods
Basic Visitors Cover | 24 hours for accident-related conditions 2 months for all hospital and medical treatments; this waiting period is waived when you purchase Australian Unity Overseas Visitors Cover before coming to Australia or within two weeks after you arrive No cover for pre-existing conditions
Mid Visitors Cover | 24 hours for accident-related conditions 2 months for all hospital and medical treatments; this waiting period is waived when you purchase Australian Unity Overseas Visitors Cover before coming to Australia or within two weeks after you arrive 24 months for all pre-existing conditions
Top Visitors Cover | 24 hours for accident-related conditions 2 months for all hospital and medical treatments; this waiting period is waived when you purchase Australian Unity Overseas Visitors Cover before coming to Australia or within two weeks after you arrive 12 months for all pre-existing conditions
Looking to buy Overseas Visitor Cover?
Get a quote
Switching from another Australian health fund
If you were previously covered by an insurer outside of Australia, you will be considered as a new member and all applicable waiting periods will apply.
If you are transferring from another registered Australian private health insurance fund, you need to purchase health cover with us within 30 days of cancelling your old cover and provide a Transfer Certificate (sometimes also called a Clearance Certificate) from your previous insurer.
Depending on the cover you purchase with us, we will recognise the following:
Non-working and working holiday visa covers: the initial two-month waiting period will be waived.
Working visa covers and extras covers: Australian Unity will recognise the waiting periods you’ve already completed under an equivalent or higher level cover.
More details related to waiting periods
Why do waiting periods exist?
If waiting periods didn’t exist, people could take out health insurance or upgrade to comprehensive cover only when they knew or suspected that they might need cover for a procedure/service, and then immediately make a claim. If these new members then cancelled (or downgraded) their membership after making a claim, their costs would have to be paid for by the fund’s long-term members. Not only is this unfair to existing members, it could also lead a fund having to increase premiums.
What is a pre-existing condition
A pre-existing condition is any illness, ailment or condition where, in the opinion of a medical advisor appointed by Australian Unity, the signs or symptoms have existed at any time during the six months up to and including the day on which you became insured under the policy—regardless of whether you were aware of it.
Depending on your level of Overseas Visitors Health Cover, you may still be able to claim on pre-existing conditions after having served a waiting period.
Find out more about pre-existing conditions.
Waiting periods for extras
If you’re going to be in Australia for an extended period, you may consider purchasing extras cover to get money back for things like going to the dentist or physiotherapist or getting a new pair of glasses.
Check your product fact sheet for full details about the waiting periods that apply to your selected level of extras cover.
Upgrading your level of cover
Upgrading your cover means increasing your level of hospital or extras benefits or reducing your excess. You may have to serve new waiting periods for services you weren’t previously covered for or for services with increased benefits payable.
You will still be entitled to the benefits payable under your previous level of cover while you are serving the waiting period for the higher benefits.
Getting your permanent residency (PR)
As far as your health insurance is concerned, a resident is someone who is eligible for full Medicare entitlements.
Once you get your permanent residency, you can switch from your Australian Unity Overseas Visitors Cover to a resident’s Private Health Insurance cover. As long as you cancel your old cover on the same day as you start your new cover, we will recognise all waiting periods you have already completed and apply those to your new cover.
If your Overseas Visitors Cover is with another health fund and you are switching to Australian Unity Private Health Insurance, you will be considered as a new member and all applicable waiting periods will apply.
To find out more about waiting periods, call us on 1300 899 739 or visit the Private Health government website.

What is a pre-existing condition?
A pre-existing condition is any illness, ailment or condition where, in the opinion of a medical advisor appointed by Australian Unity, the signs or symptoms have existed at any time during the six months up to and including the day on which you became insured under the policy—regardless of whether you were aware of it.

Pre-existing condition and waiting periods
Where applicable, the pre-existing condition waiting period applies to new members and to members upgrading their existing policy to a higher level (for example, to increase your level of hospital benefits). If you are upgrading your cover, you will still be entitled to the benefits payable under your previous level of cover while you are serving the waiting period for the higher benefits.
After you have held continuous hospital cover for the required waiting period, the pre-existing condition waiting period no longer applies and you are entitled to the full benefits under the policy.

Why is there a waiting period for pre-existing conditions?
If this waiting period didn’t exist, people could take out hospital cover or upgrade to comprehensive cover only when they knew or suspected that they might need hospital treatment and immediately make a hospital claim. If these new members then cancelled (or downgraded) their membership, their hospital costs would have to be paid for by the fund’s long-term members. Not only is this unfair to existing members, it could also lead a fund having to increase premiums.
Going to hospital during the waiting period?
For any hospital claim that might be related to a pre-existing condition, we may ask you to have a medical report completed by the first doctor you saw about the condition, such as your GP or specialist. We will then review the information and assess whether the treatment relates to a pre-existing condition.
To ensure you are not faced with any unexpected costs, you should always check that you will be covered before seeking hospital treatment. We recommend you download the Medical Report Form as soon as you know you need hospital treatment, and ask your doctor to complete it and return it to us as soon as possible. We need up to five working days to carry out the initial pre-existing condition assessment after receiving the report form.
To find out more about the pre-existing condition waiting period, call us on 13 29 39 or visit the Commonwealth Ombudsman website.

What is Gap Cover?
Australian Unity's Gap Cover can reduce or remove your out-of-pocket expenses.
We set our own schedule of fees, which is generally higher than the Government schedule. This means that when your doctor or specialist agrees to use Australian Unity's Gap Cover Scheme, we can help to pay some of the gap or the entire gap that can occur if your doctor's charge is higher than the Medicare Benefits Schedule Fee.
Gap Cover Schemes are available to all doctors who treat private patients in hospitals or day surgeries, but they don't always participate. Doctors are also free to participate in a Gap Cover Scheme on a patient-by-patient basis.
If Gap Cover won’t fully cover your participating doctor’s fees, your doctor must tell you how much you’ll have to pay in writing before treatment can begin. This is called Informed Financial Consent.
You should always ask your doctor if they will participate in the Australian Unity Gap Cover Scheme for your service prior to undergoing treatment.

To check your eligibility, please review your fact sheet or contact Australian Unity on 13 29 39.

Frequently Asked Questions
Why do premiums change each year?
While premium increases are never welcomed, they are necessary to keep pace with the rising cost of healthcare treatment. Premium increases normally occur every April across all health funds. We’re committed to keeping premium increases as low as possible whilst ensuring that our members have access to the best healthcare options when they need it.
Why is my current premium different to the amount shown in my email/letter?
The premium quoted in your letter is based on the information we had on 24 February 2026. Any changes following that date can result in changes to your current and/or future premium. Your premium can also be affected by other factors including the Australian Government Rebate on private health insurance and any Lifetime Health Cover loading. Contact us for more information specific to your membership.
Why is my current premium different to the amount I was quoted when I joined?
If you joined Australian Unity in the past 90 days, your premium may be different to what you were quoted if we’re waiting on your Australian Government Rebate form or Transfer Certificate or if the details we’ve received are different from those used for your quote when you first joined us. Contact us for more information specific to your membership.
Am I getting the Australian Government Rebate on private health insurance?
If you are claiming the Australian Government Rebate as a premium reduction, your latest ‘Health Cover Update’ communication will outline these details under the 'Your premium details' section. If you are not claiming this, visit our Government rebate page to see if you are eligible and how to apply.
Can I pay my health insurance in advance and lock in my premium amount?
Yes, if you pay your health insurance premiums in advance you could effectively lock in today's price up until 31 March 2026. This means you won’t be affected by any increase in the price of your cover for this period. Paying in advance locks in the price only, and not the terms and benefits of your cover (which may change from time to time).
I’m experiencing financial hardship, what support is available?
If you're experiencing financial hardship, please contact us to discuss the support options we have available.
My circumstances have changed and I’m not sure if my product meets my needs, what should I do?
Check your Fact Sheet to see what you’re covered for and decide if it’s still right for you or contact us for a Right Cover Check.
My premium increased more than the industry average percentage. Why did this happen?
Premium increases vary from product to product and can be attributed to a range of factors, including rising healthcare costs and the increased number and complexity of claims paid. The industry average considers premium increases across all funds, reflecting a mix of small and large changes. While it provides a general overview, individual experiences can vary depending on the specific product you hold.

title: About private health insurance
text:
Health Insurance
About Private Health Insurance
About private health insurance
Why go private?
Over 50% of Australians have private health insurance—even though Medicare provides us with one of the best public healthcare systems in the world.
That’s because private health insurance provides increased choice, convenience and flexibility.
Public Patient
Waiting List
You’re on the Public Hospital waiting list, so it might be months before you can have your surgery.
Allocated Hospital
You’ll be told which public hospital to attend for your surgery.
Appointed Doctor
The hospital will appoint the doctor who will perform your surgery.
Shared Room
For most surgeries, you’ll be in a shared room with other patients.
Private Patient
Choice of Times
Schedule your surgery in a Private Hospital at a time that suits you and your doctor.
Hospital Choices
Talk to your doctor and health fund about suitable hospitals, and then choose the one that’s right for you.
Choice of Doctor
Feel reassured by choosing the doctor to perform your surgery.
Privacy
Many private hospital covers offer private rooms.
Other benefits of going private
Private health insurance also provides cover for services generally not included under Medicare like dental, optical, physiotherapy, chiropractic, remedial massage, acupuncture and others. Many people use their private health cover to get access to services they may not otherwise be able to afford.
Plus the Australian Government has introduced a number of different measures over the years—including a rebate, a loading and a surcharge—all aimed at encouraging more people to go private. See What’s it all going to cost? to find out more about the money side of things.
So if you’re after peace of mind, shiny white teeth and possibly spending less on government loading and surcharges, private health insurance is a smart choice.
Get a quote
How does Private Health Insurance work?
There are two types of private health insurance:
Hospital insurance
Covers all or some of the costs of hospital treatment as a private patient (in both public and private hospitals) including doctor’s charges and hospital accommodation.
Extras insurance
Covers treatments generally not available under Medicare, including dental, optical, physiotherapy, chiropractic and acupuncture.
You can purchase hospital only insurance, extras only insurance, or combined hospital plus extras cover.
As a general rule, the more expensive the health cover you choose, the more hospital procedures and extras treatments will be included and the more money you’ll get back when you claim.
What cover is right for you?
Health insurance is not a one-size-fits-all proposition.
Needs change depending on things like lifestyle, life stage, health issues and financial situations. That means that a single 30-year-old looking for basic hospital and extras cover will have a different list of requirements to a young couple planning on having their first child.
Choosing health cover can be confusing and even a bit overwhelming. That’s why most health funds provide tools on their websites to help you choose the cover that’s right for you. Or if you prefer to talk to someone, you can get advice over the phone. (You can call Australian Unity on 13 29 39.)
Get a quote
What's it all going to cost?
Let’s start by looking at the Australian Government incentives and surcharges that affect the price you pay, and were designed to encourage more people to buy private health insurance.
Australian Government Rebate
This is an income- and age-tested rebate that most Australians with private health insurance can receive. It helps to reduce the cost of health insurance for both hospital and extras covers.
Read more
Medicare Levy Surcharge (MLS)
Can add between 1% and 1.5% of your income to your tax bill if you don’t have an eligible private hospital cover depending on your income.
Read more
Lifetime Health Cover (LHC)
Can add an extra 2% loading for each year you’ve gone without hospital cover over the age of 30 (up to a maximum of 70%), and takes 10 years of continuous hospital cover to remove.
Read more
All Australian Unity hospital (and hospital plus extras) covers help you avoid or reduce the MLS and LHC loading, so it’s not just the rebate that may help you to save money.
Government incentives and surcharges aside, it’s important to choose a level of cover that meets both your health and financial needs.
Don’t shop by price alone though—cheapest does not always equal best value. You’ll often find that paying just a little extra each month can actually end up saving you money, because you’re covered for more services that you’ll actually use.
After adding up the money you can receive back in claims, and considering whether any of the Government's incentives and surcharges described above apply to you, you may find that health insurance is a lot more affordable than you expected.

title:
Switching to
Australian Unity
text:
Health Insurance
Switching to Australian Unity
Health Insurance
Switching to
Australian Unity
Thinking of switching?
It’s a good idea to review your health insurance from time to time to make sure you’ve got the right level of cover at the right price.
Chances are there’s a cover out there that better suits your needs, saves you money, or both. And the good news is that it’s easy and safe to switch.
Plus when you switch to Australian Unity, you can:
Get matched with a level of cover that meets your needs and your budget, and includes services you know you’ll use.
Claim most extras back on the spot or by using our mobile claiming app (simply send a photo of your receipt).
Log in and manage to your account online, 24x7.
Get a quote
Compare covers
Switch health insurance in 3 easy steps
1. Choose your new cover from Australian Unity.
2. Sign up online or over the phone - make sure to tell us you’re switching.
3. That’s it! We’ll organise the rest.
With your permission, we’ll contact your old health fund to cancel your cover.
We’ll also get them to send us the details we need to honour waiting periods you’ve already served plus calculate your payments with the correct Lifetime Health Cover (LHC) loading.
Your old fund will usually contact you to arrange payment of any refund owing. And if you’re paying them by direct debit, it’s a good idea to let your bank know you want to cancel this deduction.
It’s safe to switch
The Australian Government guarantees “portability” protection for health insurance to make sure that you’re not disadvantaged when you switch health funds:
30 day cooling off period
If you change your mind in the first 30 days and you haven’t made any claims, you can cancel your new policy and get your money back.
Your Lifetime Health Cover (LHC) status is protected
LHC can add 2% loading for each year you’ve gone without hospital cover over the age of 30. So it’s important your previous cover is recognised and you don’t pay more than you should.
Find out more about LHC
You don’t need to re-serve waiting periods
When you switch to Australian Unity within 30 days of leaving your old health fund, and if your previous cover was of a similar or higher level, all waiting periods you’ve already served will be applied to your new cover.
You can have hospital and extras cover with different funds

title: What is the Lifetime Health Cover loading?
text:
Health Insurance
About Private Health Insurance
Lifetime Health Cover loading
What is the Lifetime Health Cover loading?
Once you turn 31, you’ve got until the following 1 July to buy private hospital cover and avoid paying the loading.
For every year you delay, you may have to pay an additional 2% on top of the cost of your private hospital cover.
Get a quote
How does Lifetime Health Cover loading work?
The Lifetime Health Cover loading was introduced by the Australian Government in July 2000 to encourage people to take out private hospital insurance at a younger age and maintain it over time.
For every year you delay, you may have to pay an additional 2% (up to a maximum of 70%) on top of the cost of your private hospital cover. The good news is that the loading doesn’t last a lifetime. Once you have held private hospital cover for 10 continuous years, the loading will be removed.
FAQs
Does everyone have to pay?
The Lifetime Health Cover loading applies if you didn’t have private hospital cover
on 1 July 2000, OR
by 1 July following your 31st birthday, whichever is later
There are some exceptions, for example if you have recently migrated to Australia or were overseas on 1 July following your 31st birthday. You can call Australian Unity on 1800 760 719 or refer to the Private Health website for information about all exclusions and special considerations that apply.
How does Lifetime Health Cover loading affect couples and families?
If you and your partner have been without cover for different lengths of time, your Lifetime Health Cover loading will be calculated by averaging out the two.
For example, if you’re paying a 4% loading, and your partner has a 10% loading, that will be averaged out to 7% on a couple or family policy.
What happens when you switch to a new health fund?
The old fund will provide your new health fund with a transfer certificate. This certificate has information about your previous cover including your Lifetime Health Cover loading plus details about any waiting periods you’ve already completed, so that these can be applied to your new cover.
That means that your Lifetime Health Cover loading moves with you.
Switch to Australian Unity
Can you have gaps in hospital cover?
To cover small gaps in private hospital cover, such as switching from one fund to another, you are able to be without private hospital cover for up to 1094 days (one day less than three years) during your lifetime, without affecting your loading.
Can you suspend your private hospital cover?
If your health fund agrees to suspend your private hospital cover for a short period (for example, while you go on an overseas vacation), your Lifetime Health Cover loading is not affected and the suspension period isn’t counted towards your 1094 days of absence.
I'm going overseas for 1 year or more, how will this affect my Lifetime Health Cover loading?
If you’re moving overseas for a continuous period of 1 year or more, you can cancel your private hospital cover without affecting your Lifetime Health Cover loading. You can even come back to visit Australia for a period of less than 90 days without it affecting your loading.
